\paragraph{Coverage notes for the daggers in the main text.}
A dagger on a number in the main text marks a run setting that differs from its neighbours in the same sentence, or a comparison set that is incomplete; each resolves to one note here.
(i) Section~\ref{sec:names_counts}, the count-removal result for GPT-4.1 mini: the names-and-counts ablation ran on its one-call row at temperature $0$ (Table~\ref{tab:cf-names-counts}); its five-draw row of Table~\ref{tab:cf-main} was not rerun under the ablation.
(ii) Section~\ref{sec:names_counts}, the count-removal result for the stronger models: GPT-5.6 Luna at five draws through the raw API and Opus 5 at one draw; GPT-5.6 Sol was not run, dropped by the registration's budget rule (Table~\ref{tab:cf-nc-strong}).
(iii) Section~\ref{sec:lookup}, the summary naming all states: GPT-4.1 mini, Haiku 4.5 and Opus 5 ran it; GPT-5.6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Sol ran the default summary only (Table~\ref{tab:cf-matched}).
(iv) Section~\ref{sec:intent}, the intent crossover: GPT-4.1 mini, Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol ran one draw and Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna five, the body reading their draw-1 column; Sol was added after an interim read of three models' rows (Table~\ref{tab:cf-intent}).
(v) Section~\ref{sec:populations}, the full obligation set: Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.6 Luna and Opus 5 completed it; the GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 runs stopped at the budget and are not scored as sets (Table~\ref{tab:x4-expansion}).

edits.old: We score separation by AUROC, the chance that a positive scores above a negative \citep{hanley1982}. Chance is $0.50$. The metric fixed in advance pools all items. Because the counterfactual set fixes the question, we also report the matched AUROC: the share of triples in which the \pn{} version outscores the \present{} version, ties counting half. It is post hoc, and we say where the two metrics disagree. A difference is \emph{reliable} when both the item-level paired and persona-grouped bootstrap intervals exclude zero. We apply no multiplicity correction, so reliable describes each comparison on its own. \emph{Within tolerance} means an absolute difference no greater than $0.05$. A gain compares the same questions with and without the summary.

edits.old:
\claim{Within a triple, a name or a count can identify the obligation.}
On the counterfactual set the \pn{} version differs from its siblings in one attribute, so its category always holds one more non-active record.
A count reader handed the question's category wins every retraction and expiry triple (a privileged reader: the models must infer the category), and the name lookup wins $82$ of the $88$ supersession triples and loses none.
For $26$ of $30$ retraction pairs and $15$ of $30$ expiry pairs that count starts at zero, so a reader can identify the store version without identifying the attribute.
What differs across readers is which of the two they use. (Appendix~\ref{app:counterfactual})

edits.old:
\claim{The two smaller models lose nothing when the counts are removed.}
Removing every count leaves mini and Haiku within $0.01$ of their intact-summary scores on either metric (mini on its single-call row).
Counts alone score reliably below names alone, by $0.14$ for each model on the matched metric ($0.12$ and $0.16$ pooled), and the whole loss falls on supersession, where the names are.
On retraction and expiry both models stay reliably below a count reader that only guesses the question's category ($0.77$ and $0.75$). (Appendix~\ref{app:counterfactual}; target-name ablation: Appendix~\ref{app:resp})
edits.new:
\claim{The two smaller models lose nothing when the counts are removed.}
With every count deleted, mini$^{\dagger}$ and Haiku stay within $0.01$ of their intact-summary scores; given the counts alone, they fall by $0.14$. Told that one more plan was cancelled without being told which, they cannot use it: on retraction and expiry both stay reliably below a count reader that merely guesses the category.

edits.old:
\claim{The three stronger models also read the counts.}
On retraction and expiry, which the default summary only counts, Luna, Sol and Opus score $0.58$ to $0.87$ on the matched metric, and none is reliably below the guessing count reader.
When the obligation's increment is moved to a sibling version with the names unchanged, all three follow it. Across the two counted states Opus falls by $0.28$ and Sol by $0.33$, and Luna falls by $0.32$ on retraction and $0.27$ on expiry, each reliable; mini and Haiku show no reliable change.
On the pooled metric the expiry falls are reliable for all three and the retraction falls for Opus alone.
Removing every count costs Luna a reliable $0.06$ and Opus $0.04$ on the pooled metric, though counts alone still score reliably below names alone for both; Sol was not run. (Appendix~\ref{app:counterfactual})
edits.new:
\claim{The three stronger models also read the counts.}
On retraction and expiry, which the default summary only counts, none of Luna, Sol and Opus sits reliably below the guessing count reader (Figure~\ref{fig:perstate}). When the obligation's extra count moves to a sibling version with the names unchanged, all three follow it, falling by $0.27$ to $0.33$ on the counted states, while mini and Haiku show no reliable change. The falls are reliable on the matched metric and, pooled, on expiry for all three and on retraction for Opus alone. Removing every count costs Luna $0.06$ and Opus $0.04^{\dagger}$ on the pooled metric, and the counts alone still score below the names alone for both; all four differences are reliable. Cancelling the hike changes only a count in the default summary, and these three readers follow it. (Appendix~\ref{app:counterfactual})

edits.old:
\claim{On the named state, no model reliably beats the lookup.}
The default summary names only supersession.
On its $88$ triples the lookup scores $0.97$ on the matched metric; Opus is $0.01$ above it, Luna and Sol $0.01$ below, and mini reliably below by $0.07$.
A sibling-name control removes list length and counts from the comparison: a fourth store version lists a different attribute of the same category, with the same counts and the same number of names.
The lookup and every model separate the \pn{} version from it at $0.88$ to $0.97$, none reliably above the lookup, while a list of meaningless tokens and the count reader fall to $0.47$ and $0.50$. (Appendix~\ref{app:counterfactual})
edits.new:
\claim{On the named state, no model reliably beats the lookup.}
Readers are compared within each triple on the matched metric, the pooled metric named where the two disagree. The default summary names only supersession; on its triples the lookup scores $0.97$, Opus is $0.01$ above it, Luna and Sol $0.01$ below, and only mini reliably below. A sibling-name control removes list length and counts with a fourth store version listing a different attribute of the same category, with the same counts and as many names. The lookup and every model pick the \pn{} version over it at $0.88$ or higher, none reliably above the lookup, while meaningless tokens and the count reader sit near chance.

edits.old:
\claim{The stronger models' lead comes from counts, and a count feature closes it within a question.}
Across all $148$ triples the lookup and Haiku score $0.78$ and mini $0.73$. Luna, Sol and Opus score $0.86$ to $0.88$, a reliable $0.08$ to $0.10$ above the lookup ($0.07$ to $0.08$ pooled), all of it from retraction and expiry, where the lookup ties every triple.
A logistic reader over the lookup's similarity and the guessed category's non-active share, fit with personas left out, scores $0.89$, reliably above the lookup, beside the three models' $0.86$ to $0.88$; we ran no equivalence test.
On the pooled metric the same reader scores $0.79$ and the three stay a reliable $0.05$ to $0.06$ above it. Their remaining edge is in pairs that cross questions and states, where their scores stay comparable and the fitted reader's do not. (Appendix~\ref{app:counterfactual})
edits.new:
\claim{The stronger models' lead comes from counts, and a count feature closes it within a question.}
Across all $148$ triples Luna, Sol and Opus score a reliable $0.08$ to $0.10$ above the lookup. All of that comes from retraction and expiry, where the summary lists no name and the lookup ties every triple. It cannot tell the cancelled hike from the planned one. A lookup given one more feature, the guessed category's share of non-active records, scores $0.89$ beside the three models' $0.86$ to $0.88$; we ran no equivalence test. Pooled across questions the gap remains: the same reader scores $0.79$ and the models stay a reliable $0.05$ to $0.06$ above it (Table~\ref{tab:cf-main}). Their scores stay comparable from one question to the next and the fitted reader's do not.

edits.old:
\claim{Long or wrong name lists weaken the readers together.}
Padding the default list to $60$ names lowers the lookup to $0.67$ on the full obligation set, and injected wrong names lower mini, Haiku and the lookup together, so short ground-truth lists do not establish robustness to longer store-written ones. (Appendix~\ref{app:counterfactual})

\claim{Long or wrong name lists weaken the readers together.}
Padding the default list to $60$ names lowers the lookup to $0.67$ on the full obligation set, and injected wrong names lower mini, Haiku and the lookup together. Short ground-truth lists therefore do not establish robustness to longer store-written ones. (Appendix~\ref{app:counterfactual})

edits.old:
\claim{The stated intent rule separates the readers.}
The supersession crossover holds the store fixed and changes the question from current value to change, using the default summary.
The change question licenses the old content.
When the rubric states that rule, Luna scores $0.96$, Sol $0.88$ and Opus $0.99$. (Appendix~\ref{app:counterfactual})
edits.new:
\claim{The stated intent rule separates the stronger readers.}
The supersession crossover holds the store fixed and changes the question from the current value to how it changed, using the default summary; the change question licenses the old content. When the rubric states that rule, Luna, Sol and Opus score $0.88$ to $0.99^{\dagger}$, while mini and Haiku, told the same rule, score $0.48$ and $0.55$. A fixed cue list matches the best model, so the test shows rule-following on cued questions and no general model advantage over deterministic intent handling.
